Consult Summary:
- 50-year-old woman with 5–6 days of a dry, continuous cough and rhinorrhea, associated with chills, myalgias, lethargy and a brief diarrheal episode; clinician impression: likely viral respiratory illness with conservative management and return precautions.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Dry, continuous cough for approximately 5–6 days, present all day and worse at night, disrupts sleep.
  - Runny nose (rhinorrhea) starting around same time.
  - Intermittent chills/shivering and generalized muscle aches.
  - Initial brief diarrhea that started with cough and resolved after the first day.
  - Cough-related throat irritation but no significant sore throat with swallowing.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Symptoms began ~5–6 days prior to visit.
  - Diarrhea occurred at onset and has resolved.
  - Cough has persisted and not improved; patient feels generally fatigued/weak.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Cough worse at night and with exertion (causes transient breathlessness when coughing).
  - Rest, fluids and time recommended; paracetamol suggested for symptomatic relief.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - No productive sputum (dry cough).
  - No ear pain, discharge, or blockage.
  - No chest pain; no baseline shortness of breath except when coughing.
  - No nausea or vomiting.
  - Appetite generally preserved.
  - Urination normal; drank increased fluids during diarrhea.
  - No rash reported.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No documented fever measurement (patient reports subjective shivering/feverish feeling but has not checked temperature).
  - No vomiting, no persistent GI symptoms after initial diarrhea.
  - No known medication allergies.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus — followed by a primary care doctor (regular checks).
- Hypertension — reportedly controlled on medication.

Medications:
- Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Lisinopril — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Conflict noted: clinician later said “Zinopril” in the transcript; patient stated Lisinopril. (See Quality checks.)
Allergies:
- No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Lives with partner; partner currently well and asymptomatic.
- Occupation: software developer (IT) — primarily sedentary work.
- Work impact: missed first day off due to feeling unwell, subsequently returned to work.
- Tobacco: former smoker; quit approximately 6 months ago.
- Alcohol: drinks wine ~3 evenings per week, typically 2–3 glasses per occasion; clinician counseling provided to reduce intake due to diabetes and hypertension.
- No other substance use mentioned.

Family History:
- Father has type 2 diabetes.
- No other family history details provided.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs documented.
- No physical exam findings documented in the transcript.

Investigations:
- No investigations or test results documented.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute viral upper respiratory infection (presumptive)
  - Assessment: Clinical impression by physician: likely viral illness causing dry cough, rhinorrhea, myalgias and transient chills; expected duration ~7–10 days.
  - Plan:
    - Conservative management: rest, increased oral fluids.
    - Symptomatic treatment: regular paracetamol as needed.
    - Occupational advice: consider taking 1–2 days off work to rest; return when able.
    - Return precautions: come back for review if not improving in 2–3 days or sooner if symptoms worsen.
    - If still feverish and cough persists/not improving, clinician may consider antibiotics for possible secondary chest infection.
    - If breathing worsens at any time, seek earlier review.
- Issue 2: Diabetes mellitus type 2 (stable under regular care)
  - Assessment: Patient reports regular follow-up with a doctor and that diabetes is under control.
  - Plan:
    - Continue current diabetes management (medication dose not documented).
    - Reinforce hydration and monitoring while unwell; follow-up with usual diabetes care as needed.
- Issue 3: Hypertension (controlled on ACE inhibitor)
  - Assessment: Patient reports hypertension controlled on Lisinopril (dose not documented).
  - Plan:
    - Continue antihypertensive medication.
    - Counseling to reduce alcohol intake to help blood pressure and diabetes control.
- General plan items:
  - Advice on alcohol reduction: clinician suggested an initial reduction strategy (example: reduce to two glasses a week then taper further) — counseling only.
  - Smoking cessation status acknowledged (quit 6 months).
  - Safety net provided: return if no improvement in 2–3 days or sooner for worsening breathing/fever.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No vital signs recorded (temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation).
  - No physical examination findings documented (chest auscultation, throat exam).
  - No medication doses/routes/frequencies documented.
  - No laboratory or imaging investigations ordered or results available.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Medication name conflict: patient stated Lisinopril; clinician later said “Zinopril.” Both statements recorded; conflict noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Transcript overall comprehensible; occasional minor disfluencies and overlapping speech but clinical content clear.
